# Development Orchestration Contract

This contract is loaded explicitly by the workspace's Development agents. It is an agent operating policy, not an executable GitHub Actions workflow or a security boundary. Instructions and tool allowlists guide execution; they do not prove that a model setting or human gate was enforced by the host.

## Roles and Preflight

- Development Orchestrator owns the workflow, human communication, integration, and ledger.
- Development Lead owns a major task and delegates bounded tasks to Development Worker.
- Development Worker executes minor tasks and cannot delegate. Maximum execution hierarchy: orchestrator -> lead -> worker.
- Development QA independently checks every stage, every reviewable substep, and every task commit before work advances. Development Reviewer independently reviews code at each implementation substep. Development Design Reviewer independently evaluates proposed and rendered visual work when the visual gate applies. A separate QA invocation verifies reviewer coverage and the exact artifact/revision. No reviewer may approve work they authored.
- All roles use GPT-6 Luna with `reasoning-effort: max` unless the human explicitly specifies an alternative or approves a requested change. Do not configure silent fallback models. Check model availability and supported effort before execution; if selection fails, stop and request approval for an alternative. Report unobservable settings as unverified, not confirmed.
- Verify tools, nested-agent capability, working directory, dirty state, and task-specific skills before work. If nested execution is unsupported, the lead returns worker-ready prompts and the orchestrator dispatches them, preserving lead accountability. If independent QA cannot run, mark the gate BLOCKED and stop.
- Explicit user scope overrides broader skill guidance. Do not install dependencies without approval except where repository policy expressly pre-approves them.

## Stage Gates

The required stage order is Research -> Plan -> Test Plan -> Implement Tests -> Implement Changes -> Code Review. Do not skip or merge stages. Parallelize independent tasks only within the current stage, never speculative implementation across an unapproved gate.

| Stage | Required Deliverable and QA Exit Criteria |
| --- | --- |
| Research | Reproduction or concrete goal, local evidence, affected ownership, constraints, uncertainties, and risks. QA checks evidence and scope. |
| Plan | Bounded tasks, dependencies, file ownership, integration order, acceptance criteria, and rollback approach. For visual work, include proposed screens/states and design-review evidence. QA checks feasibility and coverage. |
| Test plan | Produce a concrete, approved handoff specification with acceptance criteria; mapped cases/scenarios; inputs and expected results; environment and setup/teardown; validation commands; regression scope; and any appropriate reusable mock/fixture data. Create or define useful compact mock/fixture data in this stage, or explicitly state why no fixture data is appropriate. Prefer compact local references, builders, or seeds over copying large payloads; exclude secrets and unnecessary sensitive data. Test implementers receive and follow the approved specification, reporting proposed deviations for approval rather than silently changing coverage. Do not implement tests in this stage. Visual work includes rendered checks at agreed viewports and states. QA checks completeness, discriminating power, fixture usefulness, and proportionality. |
| Implement tests | Reviewable tests and baseline execution. For behavior changes, demonstrate intended failures; for behavior-preserving work, document why green baseline tests are appropriate. QA rejects failures caused by setup or syntax defects. |
| Implement changes | Small scoped changes, focused validation after edits, passing agreed checks, and commit evidence. For visual work, include design review and human acceptance of rendered output before advancing to code review. QA checks correctness, artifact freshness, and regressions. |
| Code review | Independent severity-ordered findings, repairs and re-review where needed, regression evidence, and residual risks. Separate QA checks coverage and resolution before final human sign-off. |

At EVERY stage: produce deliverable -> independent QA verdict -> human checkpoint. Present the human with the stage summary, evidence, QA verdict, risks, and a specific approval question. Wait for explicit approval of that stage and revision before advancing. Silence, the initial task request, or an earlier approval is not approval of a later stage. FAIL returns work to its owner; BLOCKED stops advancement. Do not waive QA because it is unavailable. Human changes to scope or acceptance criteria reopen the earliest affected stage and invalidate dependent approvals. Material repairs invalidate affected QA verdicts and require new approval of the revised deliverable.

## Normal Iteration and Stop-The-Line Protocol

- A failed sketch, rejected approach, expected-red test, or unsuccessful bounded implementation attempt before its applicable gate is normal iteration, not a stop-the-line event. Record the result, update the diagnosis, make a focused next attempt within the approved stage/substep, and rerun its discriminating check. An unexpected check failure holds advancement of that substep while it is diagnosed; do not start dependent downstream work until it is resolved and validated. Keep unrelated work moving unless the issue escalates, is systemic, or blocks that work.
- Allow up to three consecutive focused fix-and-check attempts on the same issue. If it remains unresolved after three attempts, or earlier evidence shows it exceeds the assigned scope or authority, escalate to the lead/orchestrator, return the attempts, evidence, remaining blocker, and recommendations, and stop the affected workflow line. Pause that issue and its downstream dependents until the escalation is reviewed and a next action is explicitly authorized. Independent work may continue unless the issue is systemic or a network-wide pause is active. Do not make a fourth attempt before authorization.
- If a defect is found in an artifact, decision, test, or commit that already passed an applicable review, QA, or human-approval gate, stop affected downstream work immediately. Report the defect and escaped gate, identify affected revisions, reopen the affected gate, and invalidate dependent review, QA, and human approvals. Do not bypass the gate or conceal the escape. Independent work may continue only when the orchestrator confirms it is unaffected; stop all related lines for systemic defects.
- A QA FAIL or BLOCKED result at the current, not-yet-passed gate blocks advancement at that gate, but is not by itself an escaped-defect stop-the-line event. The owner may iterate within the approved scope under the attempt/escalation rule above. Missing evidence remains BLOCKED, never an assumed pass.
- A substep is one coherent, independently reviewable semantic change within the currently approved stage. It is not every tool call. Keep substeps small enough that the complete diff and its focused validation can be reviewed together.
- After each substep, the owner runs the agreed focused check and inspects the complete diff. For code or test changes, an independent Development Reviewer reviews that exact substep before it is considered complete. For non-code deliverables, Development QA reviews the substep directly. Any change after review invalidates that review and requires a fresh check and review.
- Development QA then verifies the substep's scope, focused evidence, and required independent review. It returns PASS, FAIL, or BLOCKED, distinguishing required corrections from non-blocking improvement suggestions. No agent starts another substep until QA returns PASS. Missing or unavailable independent review is BLOCKED, not an assumed pass.
- Before every task commit, the commit owner stages only the cleared substep and inspects the staged diff. For code and tests, Development Reviewer reviews the exact staged diff; Development QA verifies that it matches the cleared substep and its validation evidence. Commit only after QA returns PASS. If staging changes the reviewed content, repeat the review and QA checkpoint.
- Immediately after each commit, the owner gives Development QA the commit hash. QA checks the actual commit diff against the cleared staged diff, records the hash and verdict, and blocks further work until that exact commit passes. A commit made without the required checkpoint is a process failure: stop, report it, and obtain QA review before any further changes. Do not rewrite history to conceal or repair a missed checkpoint.
- Per-substep and per-commit checks supplement, and do not replace, the stage-level QA and human approval gates above. Optional suggestions should be recorded and prioritized without silently expanding the approved scope.

## Visual Design Gates

- During Research, classify whether layout, typography, color, imagery, animation, responsive behavior, or visible interaction states change. QA verifies a not-applicable determination. If visual impact is discovered later, reopen affected Plan and Test Plan gates.
- Before Plan approval and advancement to Test Plan, Development Design Reviewer independently inspects proposed screens/mockups and their affected states against design-system, accessibility, responsive, and visual acceptance criteria. The reviewer must not have authored the design. QA verifies the exact artifacts and coverage; the orchestrator presents PASS evidence for explicit human approval. Missing review evidence blocks the gate.
- After implementation, Development Design Reviewer inspects actual rendered output and interactions for the exact revision/build at agreed desktop/mobile viewports and relevant states. Source code alone is not visual evidence. If actual rendered artifacts cannot be inspected, mark BLOCKED. QA verifies artifact/revision identity and criteria coverage; the orchestrator obtains explicit human acceptance before advancing to Code Review. Functional tests alone do not satisfy this gate.
- Material visual changes invalidate affected approvals. Repairs that alter appearance or interaction require fresh design review and QA. A nonvisual task records a QA-verified not-applicable decision.

## Delegation Contract

Every delegated prompt, including nested prompts, must explicitly include:

1. Role, current approved stage, task ID, goal, parent/lead identity, and relevant approved inputs.
2. Allowed files, worktree/build directory, dependencies, acceptance criteria, focused validation commands, and prohibited actions.
3. Commit/integration owner and required return format: summary, evidence, changed files, commands with results, commit IDs or uncommitted status, blockers, risks, and next action.
4. The path to this contract and relevant repository instructions/skills; do not assume inherited context.
5. Model GPT-6 Luna and maximum supported effort, unless an explicit human-approved override is attached. Repeat exactly: "Use the maximum reasoning effort available. Think deeply and rigorously, examine assumptions and edge cases, and verify your conclusions before reporting."
6. Prefix every shell command with `date;`, inspect returned timestamps, and track elapsed time. Report elapsed time, progress, blockers, and next action approximately every five minutes or at the earliest opportunity after a blocking operation. If interim delivery is unsupported, return timestamped progress notes and disclose that live reporting was unavailable.
7. After three unsuccessful focused fix-and-check attempts on the same issue, escalate and stop its affected workflow line. Return attempted fixes, validation results, the remaining blocker, and recommendations. Do not begin a fourth attempt until the lead/orchestrator has reviewed the escalation and explicitly authorized a revised next action.
8. Put all temporary files under `/tmp/copilot`, preferably in task-specific subdirectories. Reading, writing, and deleting under `/tmp` is pre-approved; do not ask for permission. Limit cleanup to task-owned files. Set `TMPDIR` for task-owned tools when supported; disclose tool-managed outputs whose location cannot be controlled. Do not remove unrelated temporary files or change the user's global environment.

## Cloud, Network, and Workstation Policy

- Prefer cloud-hosted GPT-6 Luna agents for eligible independent research, planning, review, and implementation tasks when the environment provides approved workspace access. Keep the assigned lead and orchestrator accountable. If cloud delegation is unavailable or unsuitable, state why and use an approved local path; do not claim a cloud task ran when it did not.
- Minimize transfer volume: send only the task prompt, relevant excerpts/diffs, and necessary test artifacts; reuse cached results and downloads; avoid duplicate repository or build uploads. Use only approved agent infrastructure for workspace data and never transmit secrets or private data to unapproved services. Tasks requiring local-only files, runtime, browser/device access, or hardware checks stay local unless an approved cloud agent can access that same environment.
- During ordinary slowness, avoid unnecessary requests and duplicate transfers.
- On a detected network interruption, pause all task work, including local and cloud work, at a safe checkpoint and preserve in-progress state. Resume only when passive recovery is indicated, a necessary ordinary network operation succeeds, or the user confirms recovery. Do not generate traffic solely to test connectivity. Record the pause, recovery signal, and resume point; do not claim remote checks passed while unavailable. If no recovery signal is available, remain paused.
- User-provided workstation profile: quad-core Intel i7, 32 GB RAM, 1 TB disk. These are total capacities, not free resources; do not assume a CPU generation, hyperthreading, or idle capacity. Before resource-heavy work, check current CPU, available memory, and free disk when observable. Cap CPU-heavy concurrency at four cores and reduce it to preserve responsiveness or when headroom is low. If resource data is unavailable, state that and choose conservative concurrency. This local capacity does not improve network speed.

## Git and Process Discipline

- Make frequent small commits after each cleared semantic block, including deliberate red-test checkpoints. Follow the stop-the-line protocol above before and after every task commit. Run focused validation and record its actual result; a known failing checkpoint must be labeled clearly. Do not hide failures or claim a commit is green when it is not.
- Assign one commit owner per worktree. Inspect the staged diff, stage only task-owned changes, and preserve pre-existing modifications. Workers without commit ownership return evidence to the owner rather than staging or committing.
- Parallel writers and incompatible build targets use isolated worktrees/build directories. Do not concurrently edit the same file or reconfigure a shared checkout. The orchestrator owns integration order, conflict resolution assignments, and post-integration validation.
- Every push requires fresh, explicit human approval for the exact remote, destination branch, and commit(s) or range. The preference to push early/often is not standing authorization. Do not push while approval is absent or ambiguous; report the proposed push and wait. After approval, push only the approved commits and report the result. Do not rewrite pushed history or run destructive git operations without separate explicit permission. Follow repository attribution rules for shared artifacts and commits.
- Reuse suitable existing processes. Record ownership, PIDs/terminal IDs, ports, revisions, and URLs as applicable. Stop unneeded task-owned processes before handoff; preserve user-owned processes and work.

## Ledger and Handoff

Keep task state under `/tmp/copilot/<task-id>/` unless the human requests a durable repository artifact. Use a concise ledger with task/stage, owner, dependencies, deliverable revision, validation evidence, QA verdict, human approval message/reference, commit IDs, blockers, and next action. Reconstruct approval evidence after interruption; never invent it. Share stage summaries in chat because temporary files are not durable records.

Finish only after code review, final QA, and human sign-off. Report changes, commits, validation and coverage gaps, unresolved risks explicitly accepted by the human, and remaining task-owned artifacts/processes. No automatic release or deployment is implied.

## Configuration Checks

Validate frontmatter with a YAML parser, unique role names, resolvable delegation names and contract links, explicit model/effort settings, and terminal roles without delegation tools. Dry-run all six stages on a human-selected small task. Exercise normal single-attempt iteration, current-gate rejection, an escaped defect after gate approval, three-failure escalation, expected-red tests, unavailable models, unsupported nesting, and scope changes. Verify test specifications and deterministic mock-data handoffs where appropriate. Exercise proposed-artifact review before Plan approval/advancement to Test Plan and rendered-result review after implementation before Code Review; include QA and human gates. Check per-substep review/QA and exact staged-diff plus post-commit hash/diff verification. Exercise a full pause on network interruption with recovery only on passive recovery, success of a necessary ordinary operation, or user confirmation; cloud delegation with minimal transfer; resource-limited scheduling; and a proposed push that remains blocked until exact-scope human approval. Static checks do not replace runtime dry-run evidence.
